are no greater than they are in the United States, especially when you consider the dust bowls that were created in various parts of that country.
Reference has been made to a study made by the late R. E. Motherwell entitled "A Study of Crop Insurance", published in 1944. I notice that on page 19 he states that it might be said that the experience with allrisk crop insurance in the United States was disappointing. Note that that statement was made in 1944.
Crop insurance in the United States was instituted in 1938, and from that year until 1944 very heavy losses were suffered. During that period there were losses of about $71 million, $7 million being for wheat alone. In 1944 the act was suspended. Therefore in making an analysis of crop insurance in the United States it certainly would not be fair to base it upon the period 1938 to 1944, during which crop insurance was in its infancy and heavy losses were suffered. An interesting point to note is that after 1944 a number of radical changes were made in the act, and during the past six years the act has operated most successfully.
As I say, the act was first instituted in 1938. No private insurance was available in the United States, as in Canada, except hail insurance. During the first year wheat only was insured but in the following year cotton, flax, corn and tobacco were included in the scheme. Insurance could be for 75 or 50 per cent of the average long-term yield. The contracts were for one year only, meaning that the insurance had to be sold every year, increasing the expenses of selling the insurance.
At that time adjustments were in the hands of local committees, and it was found quite often that the local committees were far more interested in paying large indemnities to the farmers than in trying to really assess the actual losses. As I have pointed out, during that period from 1938 to 1944 the losses were $71 million, of which $7 million was for wheat.
I should like to refer to the various changes that were made in 1946 and 1947, and which are applicable today. Now insurance is allowed only up to 75 per cent of the average long-term yield or the actual amount invested in the current crop, whichever is the lesser of the two. Coverage and premium rates are set by areas instead of on an individual basis. Adjustments are of course on an individual basis. A local agent is appointed in each county to sell and service the insurance instead of having it handled by local committees as in the past. The adjusters who

Supply-Agriculture
set the losses are responsible directly to the state authority instead of to the local committee.
Largely as a result of these changes there has been considerable improvement in the over-all position of the insurance corporation, and during the past six years we find that the premiums and indemnities have been virtually in balance. This is in spite of the fact that during the past three years they have had heavy crop losses. In the report to congress in 1953 by the federal crop insurance corporation we find this on page 1:
The 1953 losses were the heaviest of three successive years of serious drought losses under the crop insurance program.
And then at page 5:
The most significant fact revealed by this chart from the standpoint of sound insurance operations is that premiums and indemnities are virtually in balance for this six-year period.
A table shows that during that six-year period the premiums were $106-5 million while the indemnities amounted to $106-6 million. In other words there was only one-tenth of a million dollars lost during that whole six-year period. It is interesting to note that in connection with wheat alone there was actually a profit of $1-3 million, so the losses shown were on crops other than wheat.
Roughly, crop insurance in the United States is put into effect by guaranteeing the farmer a certain amount of production. If his production falls below that amount he is indemnified for the shortage. For instance, if a farmer insures 100 acres at a yield of 10 bushels per acre; if for insurance purposes the price is set at $2 per bushel and then he produces only 400 bushels, the shortage of 600 bushels would be made up to him at $2 per bushel, or a total of $1,200. The first application for insurance must be made before the closing date, which is a short time before planting; but once the first application has been made the insurance continues in force until it is cancelled. After planting the farmer must fill out certain forms and pay the premium, but he may delay paying the premium until his harvest operations.
Considerable interest has been shown in the premium rate for insurance in the United States. Some people are of the opinion that the cost is prohibitive to the farmer, but the actual figures prove the opposite to be true. The premium rate varies considerably across the country, but the average is $75. We find that some large farms paid over $1,000, while small farms would pay $5 or $6. The actual percentage figures are quite interesting. Taking 1953, which was a year of quite

heavy losses, the average premium for all types of insurance bought was 6-2 per cent of the protection afforded. The average premium that actually would have been required if all losses had been met would have been 6-7 per cent of the protection afforded. That is for all crops. On wheat alone, in 1953 the average premium paid was 8-5 per cent of the protection afforded. If all losses had been met in 1953 it would have required a premium of 8-7 per cent of the protection afforded.
It must be remembered that many farmers in the west pay considerably more than that for hail insurance alone. I think hon. members will agree that these are most moderate rates. I am satisfied that under an all-risk system of crop insurance in western Canada the hail insurance rates would be brought down considerably. If you had an insurance scheme applicable to all areas I am satisfied you would get the insurance rate down.
The reason for this is obvious. Those people who insure against damage by hail are chiefly those who feel they might suffer losses from hail. Then, farmers hesitate to insure against hail because they know if they have a crop failure from other causes than hail they are not going to be able to pay their hail insurance premium in the fall. I am sure if there were a system of insurance covering all hazards you would have a wide coverage in western Canada and your rates would be similar to those in force in the United States.
The federal crop insurance corporation is an agency of the United States department of agriculture, with a capital stock of $100 million in the form of a revolving fund. That $100 million is subscribed by the federal government. It covers all hazards except theft, neglect and poor prices. Insurance is not written unless there are 200 applications within a county, or unless 30 per cent of the total number of farmers in the county make application for it. Insurance is on a voluntary basis. Premiums are required to be set at a level that it is believed will be adequate to cover losses that may occur.
Insurance is not available in all counties. In counties where the hazard is very great, insurance is not written and the farmers there have to depend upon some form of relief measure. In Canada, of course, areas like that would continue to be covered by the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. In most counties insurance is written only for one type of crop. On the other hand, there are cases where two crops have been insured under a form of insurance known as multiple insurance.

It is interesting to note that insurance covers the majority of the heavy wheat producing areas in the United States. In 1954, some 803 counties were insured out of a total of 3,000; that is, more than a third of a million farmers were insured. Wheat is the main crop that is insured.
Some may ask the reason there are not more farmers under crop insurance in the United States. The answer is that crop insurance in the United States is still on an experimental basis, and therefore the government are not willing to allow all counties to insure. But the area is being steadily extended. I should like to quote from the report by the federal crop insurance corporation on that question. This is found on page 22 of their directive, referring to the period after 1944:
As a result of the new legislation and other changes made in the insurance and its operation the financial experience improved greatly on wheat and the experience on flax, tobacco and corn was quite satisfactory. However, large losses occurred on cotton insurance in 1945 and 1946, primarily as a result of droughts in the southwest. By the end of 1946, over three-fourths of the original capital of $100 million had been lost. However, a profit of about $8-5 million was made in 1947 recovering part of these losses, but not before the congress had reviewed the operations in the light of the 1945 and 1946 experience and had decided to reduce the program to more of an experimental basis. Insurance was authorized in only a limited number of counties. There were 200 wheat counties and 56 cotton counties and a smaller number of counties for the other crops. Provision was made that insurance should not exceed generally the investment in the crop in the area. While the number of counties was restricted, the congress indicated that this experimental period should be used to develop insurance for other types of crops so that when the insurance was offered again in some of these counties, it could be offered not necessarily on wheat or cotton but on the crops that provided the major source of income for the farmers there. Since then insurance has been started on beans and citrus fruits and with the multiple crop insurance started in 1948, insurance has been applied to many different crops . . .
The insurance experience since 1948 has been more satisfactory. Insurance operations since that time might be considered as more intensive rather than extensive operations. Congress on several occasions has reviewed the program and has authorized gradual expansion of the number of counties where insurance is offered.
It points out that it was brought down for a short time to 200 counties; that was all the counties where the corporation was allowed to write the insurance. That has now been expanded to 803 counties, and there is every indication they will be able to continue to expand the operation of the insurance. When we say that, comparatively speaking, there is not a large percentage of the farms in the United States insured, I would point out that it is largely as a result of the insurance corporation keeping its operations down rather than the farmers refusing to insure under it.
Supply-Agriculture
The report shows quite conclusively that all-risk crop insurance can be provided at a reasonable cost so long as you exclude the submarginal, heavy risk areas. Those areas have to come under some form of relief measure, and in Canada they could continue to come under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I would suggest that any attempt to bring some of these submarginal areas into a crop insurance scheme would break that insurance program. I am convinced that allrisk crop insurance could operate in Canada, but it will have to be underwritten by the federal government in the same way crop insurance is underwritten by the federal government in the United States. It is interesting to note that the late Mr. R. E. Motherwell, in the study he made of crop insurance in 1944, came to the same conclusion. On page 35 he states:
Since the three prairie provinces are so closely associated in agricultural production, any attempt at crop insurance could best be handled by federal administration affecting the area now affected by the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Admittedly, insurance is not a federal matter but this problem clearly seems one requiring a broader scope than just one province.
The part played by crop insurance in the United States has been important. I believe it could play just as important a part in this country. I should like to quote from the federal crop insurance corporation's report to congress in 1953, upon the effect the system has had upon the general economy of the country. I quote from page 1:
The service to individual farmers and the nation that a soundly operated crop insurance program can provide is strongly emphasized by crop disasters such as resulted from the widespread 1953 drought. This program utilizes established business principles of insurance to enable farmers to do for themselves what otherwise requires emergency assistance from the government. The value of this service is not measured solely by the indemnities paid. Crop insurance policies provide security for crop loans which often cannot otherwise be obtained from private sources. Moreover, the protection provided by crop insurance is not limited to the insured farmer but extends through him to the community in which he lives and the channels of trade through which his crop or indemnity dollars pass. The need for such insurance has increased in recent years as the operating capital required for successful farming has increased. There is still much improvement to be made in all-risk crop insurance before it can attain the goal of providing all farmers the opportunity to insure the money spent on crop production against loss from causes beyond their control. The attainment of such a goal will require the development of crop insurance protection on additional crops and in areas where the program is not currently operating.
Those remarks could apply to Canada just as well as they apply to the United States. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture would say they apply equally as well to the operation of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and I would agree with him; but on the other

Supply-Agriculture
hand the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was never intended to provide crop insurance on a wide scale, nor can it do so.
In view of the high cost involved in producing crops, there is a need today for crop insurance that will make it possible for the farmer to insure the money he has invested in the production of the current crop. At the present time unemployment insurance gives stability to labour. Crop insurance would be able to give a great deal of stability to the farmer. The government contributes to unemployment insurance, and there is no reason why the government should not be prepared to at least underwrite a system of crop insurance. It might mean that in many years they would not have to make any contribution at all. It would merely mean setting up a revolving fund which could be used in case of catastrophe.
There are minimum wages to protect labour. Support prices in the same way should protect agriculture. I would suggest that with adequate support prices and a system of crop insurance we could stabilize farm income; and if you stabilize the farm income you will be helping to stabilize the whole Canadian economy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as whip of the party I am perhaps not supposed to make speeches. Possibly this would be particularly so with respect to the first item of the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture. I am supposed to be something like the small boy, to be seen but not heard. However, there is a matter that I think is of sufficient importance to the members of the House of Commons and to the country that they should know more about it, and I am taking advantage of this opportunity, on the minister's estimates, to speak of it. I think I am justified in doing so because it involves agricultural policies and, as well, certain features in the estimates of the minister's own department.
I refer at this time to the serious flooding conditions now existing along the Assini-boine river east of the city of Portage la Prairie and affecting farm lands in the municipality of Portage la Prairie, Cartier, St. Francois Xavier and Macdonald. At the present time there are well over two townships of land completely inundated and which will not be seeded this year. In addition the village of Elie is also in danger of being flooded.
This is the second flood in part of this area this year. The first was caused by an ice jam during the spring breakup. It forced the evacuation of about 300 families in the middle of the night on the south side of the city of Portage la Prairie, as well as endangering the R.C.A.F. station south of the city. The second

flood is of a much more serious character and, of course, of much longer duration. This second flood now under way is due to a heavy rainstorm in the upper reaches of the Assini-boine river and the Qu'Appelle valley in the province of Saskatchewan. Apart from the ice jam which occurred earlier, there would have been no serious flooding along the Assiniboine river this year had it not been for this critical storm in the province of Saskatchewan.
I made a trip to my constituency to view the flood and damage caused by the ice jam during the Easter recess. During the beginning of this week, along with the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for St. Boniface, I spent the greater part of three days looking over what is now taking place.
The Assiniboine river drains an area of nearly 60,000 square miles, which includes a large part of eastern Saskatchewan and all of western and northern Manitoba and includes the run-offs of the Duck mountain, the Riding mountain and the Nut mountain. Its main tributaries are the Souris river, the Qu'Appelle river and the .Minnedosa river. All the water from this area must flow down the Assiniboine river and meet the Red river at the city of Winnipeg. Should those two rivers meet in full flow it could be an extremely serious matter to the city of Winnipeg.
I should like to indicate for a moment just what I saw on this last visit. I saw thousands and thousands of sandbags. I saw volunteers placing those sandbags in an attempt to save the dikes and prevent a break-through. I saw bridge planks and timbers packed in weak places. I saw as well the army taking its part in attempting to protect the dikes and prevent any additional flooding. Perhaps I can describe it best by saying that the Assiniboine river, in full flow, was carrying
20.000	cubic feet of water per second. There was a break-through on the south side about
1.000	feet in width. Through that breakthrough, at its full flow, one-quarter of the river was passing, going down to the south and east over those high-class farm lands in that area.
That is the picture we saw out there. Just how those men have been able to do the amount of work that has been done on those dikes in order to try to protect them is something I do not know. I am surprised that we did not hear of more people suffering heart attacks, exhaustion or something of that nature. That tremendous job was done, and it was done mostly on a voluntary basis.
I should like to say a word or two about the history of this river. It has been classed

as a navigable stream, and it is also an interprovincial stream. Until now, so far as any protective works along it are concerned, that has been considered a federal responsibility. Flooding has not been uncommon on this river. As a matter of fact, as far back as 1916 efforts were made to provide a certain amount of protective work against flooding. It was then done under the department of the interior, and for a while under the federal Department of Public Works. The records show that some $300,000 was spent on protective works in the lower reaches of this river between 1923 and 1950. Since that time I have persuaded the Minister of Agriculture to take this river under the jurisdiction of his department, and the repair work since then has been done under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. Since that time about $55,000 a year has been expended on protective works.
Did it take your persuasion to get him to act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
No, he was very glad to do so in that he looked upon it as a reclamation job that the prairie farm rehabilitation organization was well able to undertake. I need not tell my friends from Manitoba that in its lower reaches this river is about as crooked as anything one can imagine; that the soil is of an alluvial character which erodes very easily, and as a consequence, because of these crooks in the river, there is continual erosion leaving it open to overflowing its banks at any low places. That is the problem that has so far been faced in an attempt to prevent the river from overflowing its banks.
May I say also that major floods have been reported on this river in the past. I am told that the most serious floods in the recollection of the present generation occurred back in 1922 and 1923. But I know, as do others who settled there, that there has been serious flooding in the interval. As a matter of fact, in recent times a flood or the danger of a flood has occurred about every second or third year. The problem has therefore become one of major concern. I repeat that this affects the best land in Canada, namely, the lower reaches of the Portage plain. The matter of water control in our province is a critical one in that we are perhaps the lower part of the run-off region from such a large area both to the south and to the west. It is one of the problems that our province has continually been facing. Steps have been taken to try to effect a remedy, but I am afraid something more will have to be done.
Supply-Agriculture
Hon. members will recall the flood of 1950 at Winnipeg. Immediately thereafter a survey commission was set up to see if they could establish some means of protecting this flooded area. The report of the commission was published in 1952 and is known as the conservation and flood control report on the Assiniboine river. I commend the reading of the report to hon. members. It is one of the most readable, practical and scientific reports I have had the experience of reading and is most understandable from a layman's point of view at least. I am going to take the liberty this afternoon, for the benefit of those outside the province of Manitoba who may not be too familiar with the circumstances in our province, of referring to certain parts of the report. First of all I refer to a paragraph on the introductory page which is in the following words:
The following study of the Assiniboine basin problems has been preceded over the past 60 years by various other studies carried out by different agencies. During 1886 an examination of the Assiniboine river was made by the Department of Public Works of Canada with a view to ascertaining the cause of annual floods. As far back as 1920, a scheme was evolved whereby a canal was to be dug from the Assiniboine river somewhere near Portage la Prairie to lake Manitoba. After the floods of 1922 and 1923, the federal departments of public works and of interior undertook various investigations. Their reports concluded that control of floods was possible only by a combination of detaining a portion of the flood waters in the upper reaches of the river and the construction of dikes. The only construction carried out, however, was the building of dikes between Portage and Winnipeg.
I also wish to refer to another part of the introductory section of the report and read a paragraph at page 7 having something to do with the creation of the problem that now exists. It reads:
At the end of the glacial period the topography of the Assiniboine basin was very similar to what it is at the present time, but the water conditions were entirely different. The receding glaciers released tremendous quantities of water, and at the same time blocking off the drainage to the north. A glacial lake stood at the foot of the ice fields extending southward until it found an outlet along the present course of the Minnesota river, thus draining off into the Mississippi basin. The Saskatchewan river was forced by the ice barrier to overflow at the Elbow into the Qu'Appelle valley. Thence the river took its course east, entering the Assiniboine river at the present site of Lazare. From there on the combined flow of the Saskatchewan, the Qu'Appelle and the Assiniboine rivers eroded a very wide and deep valley down to the glacial lake Agassiz.
I simply refer to that as indicating part of the early history of the developments that have taken place with respect to the entire drainage basin of the Assiniboine river. I want to refer now to a section having to do

Supply-Agriculture
with the conclusions in the introductory part of the report. This is what it says, as found at page 17:
Most of the flood water of the Assiniboine river tends to come from the Riding mountain, Duck mountain and Nut mountain, as shown on figure 1. This part of the drainage basin is roughly 25 per cent of the total area of 59,000 square miles. There are no exceptionally high floods in the Assiniboine valley on record since 1900. The information about the extreme flood of 1882 is vague. From a statistical point of view it can be expected that flood peaks about twice as large as the ones of 1922 or 1923 will occur within a hundred year period.
I might say that in more recent times, perhaps owing to the removal of bush and the extension of drainage, flood possibilities have become much greater. That leads me to say something about what is the main purpose of my remarks this afternoon, having to do with the flooding conditions of the Assiniboine river. X should outline to the committee what the policy has been up to now. I said a while ago that this was looked upon as a navigable stream under the jurisdiction of the federal government. The policy that has been followed has been an effort to protect that area most subject to flooding by dikes along the lower places and by straightening out bends in the river by cutting through the crooks. It has not been entirely satisfactory but it has provided a large measure of control. No other step of a practical nature was seriously suggested until the report of this commission was submitted two years ago. I have heard others talk about other possibilities of providing protection, but from the engineering standpoint none of the suggestions has met with engineering approval. The report of the flood control commission that examined the whole problem, and to which I have referred, suggested three ways of providing protection. One was the building of a large storage reservoir at Russell. The second was to build a cut-off from the Assiniboine river, in the neighbourhood of Portage la Prairie, to lake Manitoba. The third was to continue the diking program on a much extended scale. There was also some consideration given to the possibilities of a further diversion near the vicinity of the city of Winnipeg.
No matter which one of these undertakings is considered each one of them is a costly undertaking, so costly that I doubt very much if it would be undertaken at the local level at all. So far as the cut-off to lake Manitoba is concerned, that would go through some of the most valuable land in the province of Manitoba. It would have to pass through a highway and two or three railway tracks. Having regard to the fact that lake Manitoba itself is about 3-5 feet above

normal level, this project could hardly be entertained at this time unless there was some assurance that the level of lake Manitoba could be lowered in order to protect those who live along its shore line.
This brings me to the point where I have come to the conclusion, after living with this problem for 20 years, that a start should be made on providing for protective works upstream. As I review this report I believe the logical location for such a protective undertaking would be at Russell in Manitoba. This, too, is a very large undertaking but I do not believe we can neglect the fact that something of a permanent character should be undertaken. I am prepared to admit that even the building of a dam at an estimated cost two years ago of $6 million is not a guarantee of complete protection against flooding in the lower reaches of the Assiniboine river. But I do submit it would provide a measure of protection in most years of flooding, and on that ground I feel it should be given serious consideration.
The reservoir that would be built up behind this dam would, I might say, be largely in Saskatchewan and only partly in Manitoba. When the proposed dam is in place, it is estimated, the reservoir of water will stretch back into Saskatchewan for 50 miles and will be from one mile to two miles wide. It will contain about 450,000 acre feet of water.
Is that 50 miles from Russell or 50 miles into Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
It is 50 miles from Russell. The drainage area is estimated to be 7,600 square miles. According to this report the engineers have designed a reservoir which, at flood level, would contain approximately 600,000 acre feet of water. With the spillway operating and a normal water level, it would be
450.000	acre feet. The amount of water estimated to be ordinarily in storage is
350.000	acre feet. The surface area at flood level would be about 22,000 acres.
This is a major undertaking, and I am not suggesting to the minister it could be undertaken in his ordinary prairie farm rehabilitation estimates alone. It should be looked upon as a major project of interest to practically all of the northern half of Manitoba, and particularly the Assiniboine river valley. This proposition will have the advantage of protecting the city of Brandon, the city of Portage la Prairie and the R.C.A.F. station located there, as well as the flooded lands lower down against most of the flood conditions that have arisen in recent years. That is one feature of it. In addition to that the holding back of the water, and allowing it out gradually during the summer, would

also be of particular advantage to places like Brandon and Portage la Prairie for their water and sewage projects. I might add that now that the two airports at Portage la Prairie are going to be tied in with the city's water supply, it is of considerable interest to them as well.
I am suggesting this afternoon that while this is a costly undertaking, it is nonetheless a means of making a start in relieving the flood condition that recurs with all too great frequency on the Assiniboine river. I am not unmindful of what is involved in this undertaking. I go farther and say to the house that one of the problems today is not the cost of building the dam itself but the cost of removing or changing the location of existing public utilities and things of that nature. According to the engineers' report the actual cost of the dam is not too unreasonable, but the project involves as well the moving of a railway, the raising of three roads, the building of several bridges and the purchase of the land.
Now, that may seem like a big undertaking; but, having regard to the land that is flooded in the lower reaches and knocked out of production, I think something of this nature has to be considered. It may well be that the cost feature of it will shock some people. However, according to this report the cost, as compared to similar undertakings in the United States, is not unreasonable. The per acre cost of this undertaking is estimated at $15 per acre foot of water. The average weighted cost of 168 flood control projects in the United States according to this report, based on the 1952 price index, is estimated to be $60 per acre foot of water storage. On that basis, by comparison with other undertakings that have been proceeded with, the cost of this project is not excessive.
This afternoon, Mr. Chairman, I am urging the construction of this dam at Russell. I believe it would be beneficial, particularly in dry periods, in retaining a supply of water in the upper reaches of the river in Saskatchewan. It will provide also a large measure of control against flooding and will supply a more normal flow of water during low water periods on the Assiniboine river, all the way from the dam to the city of Winnipeg, helping the water supplies of those places along the way.
It of course takes time for undertakings of this nature to be accepted. I know that there will be a good deal of concern expressed by people in the area that is likely to be flooded, if this project is proceeded with. However, I am happy to say that there is an organization known as the Assiniboine river
Supply-Agriculture
control organization set up to press this particular matter of the flooding of the Assiniboine river. It has held two or three meetings. I have before me a report of the discussions that took place at their last annual meeting held only a few weeks ago. I might say that this meeting was representative of the reeves and councillors of most of the municipalities along the Assiniboine. I find in reading the report a very general recognition of the problem and an indication of willingness to co-operate, provided of course that those whose properties might be taken over or subject to damage would be compensated. That is the general tenor of the report. I was going to read certain sections of it, but I do not think I need to do so, more than to quote one or two observations:
Mr. Lacroix of Cartier municipality said this:
"I believe we need the dam, but we do need some dikes as well and some straightening of the river, in order that dikes will be of some permanent use. Some farmers have donated as much as 30 to 40 acres for diking purposes."
That brings me to another point in connection with the Assiniboine river. The department has been doing the work of diking and straightening the river, and providing money for that purpose; but the land has been provided either by the farmers or by the municipalities. In some cases this land has not been forthcoming; and in certain places where dikes should have been built the farmers were not prepared to give the land, or even to sell it, to the municipality.
I am suggesting to the minister therefore that, having regard to the vote already in the estimates, consideration should be given to exercising expropriation proceedings or something of that nature to acquire this land for the dikes and cut-offs, and pay for it out of this vote, so that a logical and more reasonable process of diking and straightening the river could be undertaken. That has appealed to me as reasonable; and I think the farmers in the area have donated about all the land they can be expected to donate.
I was going to make one reference to the flood, and at this point I should like to hand two pictures to the minister. The first I would hand him is a picture showing the flooding of the Assiniboine river where it crosses the highway between Elie and Oakville. The second picture is one of the places I saw myself. It is at the break where the Assiniboine broke through the dikes and is now going across country. I said that a quarter of the river was going through this break. However, that amount is lessening at the moment, and the last information I had was

Supply-A griculture
that the flow was down to about 1,000 cubic feet per second. Men were starting out to plug that hole. I would give a picture of this to the minister, as an indication of the location of the break, as well as its extent. The land below that point is flooded.
My reference now will be to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which admittedly has not been too popular in Manitoba. There have been many complaints about its application, on the ground that it does not meet our circumstances as satisfactorily as some feel it should. The hon. member for Acadia has just referred to crop insurance. Well, we do not have a scheme of crop insurance in operation up to now; but in this area, in the coming summer, the land will be flooded and no crop will be seeded. As a consequence there will be no basis upon which to establish the seeded acreage as a basis for prairie farm assistance. The area will be large; certainly in Manitoba it will be more than two townships.
I am wondering if the minister would entertain or could work out some amendment or some change in the application of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act whereby, in large flooded areas such as we have in Manitoba, these flooded areas could be made eligible for prairie farm assistance payments. Their circumstances are certainly as critical as those who are in the dried out areas; yet, because of the application of the act, they cannot qualify technically for assistance because they are unable to seed. I am suggesting therefore that, with these abnormal conditions developing, perhaps a measure of relief could be provided under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, whereby large areas- townships or half townships-might be included as those entitled to assistance under the act.
I know I have talked on only one subject, but I did so because it is of special interest to Manitoba, including Winnipeg; and naturally it is of particular interest to my own constituency. I think my suggestion, that of building a reservoir at Russell, Manitoba, is a sound one, and I hope that it will be entertained favourably. It would be of advantage not only as a conservation project but also to prevent flooding. It would at the same time provide an added supply of water to places at points lower downstream during periods of dry weather.
I submit this in all earnestness as a first practical and reasonable approach to the flooding conditions in the Assiniboine river.

Mr. Chairman, if I might speak for a moment-and I will not be more than that-I would point out that, of course,

the report referred to, which I have here, is one which was issued as the result of an investigation we ordered some time ago. That is, it had to be agreed to and ordered by myself as minister. It has been carried out by P.F.R.A. engineers. The matter has been under consideration, and will continue to be under consideration.
I am not in a position at the moment to say whether it will be proceeded with. The very amount which is involved indicates that it could not be proceeded with under the votes we have had for P.F.R.A. If it were going to be considered at all it would have to be considered under what have been known generally as a vote for large projects, to which my hon. friend refers.
So far as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is concerned, let me say that we have been giving consideration to possible amendments. There are difficulties in connection with amending P.F.A.A. to take care of some of the difficulties the farmers have. Nevertheless we have been looking at it and attempting to work out something which would be satisfactory, and we will continue to do so.

Mr. Chairman, most hon. members who have spoken so far in this debate have suggested that the minister should spend more money for one purpose or another. I am going to suggest that he should spend less on one item. I wish to comment briefly this afternoon on the Canadian butter situation. I realize quite well that probably few members will agree with my views, but one of the advantages of sitting in the independent corner, sir, is that I embarrass no one but myself.
I am going to maintain this afternoon that the government's present butter policy is shortsighted and economically unwise. Not only is this policy costing the taxpayers several millions of dollars; 1 submit it is also resulting in thousands and thousands of Canadians, who otherwise would be eating butter,

switching to margarine and similar substitutes. As a result, the butter industry today is in a serious predicament. The government has set the floor price at an unrealistic level if butter is to compete with substitutes.
There has been a steady piling up of storage butter over the past several years. According to figures which I obtained from the minister's department, on May 1, 1952, the government had in storage approximately 17 million pounds of butter; on May 1, 1953, this surplus had increased to approximately 27 million pounds; on May 1, 1954, the amount on hand was 33 million pounds; and as at May 1 of this year the figure had reached the record high of over 50 million pounds.
Butter is a perishable product and if you keep it on hand too long it is likely to go bad. That is precisely what I fear may happen, if our surplus continues to increase. If this butter should go bad, then the taxpayers will be given a bill for additional millions of dollars. In view of this fact, it seems to me that parliament should re-examine our whole floor price policy in connection with butter which the government inaugurated a short time ago.
I realize that the minister has been concerned about the problem. In an effort to do something about it, last February he introduced a program of selling butter to hospitals, orphanages, et cetera, at a discount of about 21 cents per pound. After four months of trial, it is pretty obvious that this scheme has not been too successful, because according to a return tabled in the house, page 3656 of Hansard of May 11, only 932,523 pounds had been sold up to May 6. That would indicate to me that this scheme has not been too successful. Month after month our butter surplus continues to increase. Probably a great part of this butter sold to institutions would have been sold anyway.
Just to put the latest figure on the record, as of May 27 the figure was 1,299,611 pounds, which I agree is not as high as I had hoped it would be.

That is a slight improvement, but when you compare it with the total amount of butter in storage it is pretty small. Last week the minister announced another step in an effort to get rid of some of our butter surplus. He said that the government would sell storage butter at 56 cents a pound. Of course this means that the taxpayer will have to absorb the difference. I do not think that this step will solve the problem any more than the first effort.
Supply-Agriculture

This is just a repetition of
what we did last year and the year before for a period at the beginning and it will be cut off some time later.

I agree, and that is why I
say that such action is not going to be any more successful this year than it was in 1954 in disposing of our surplus. I do not need to tell the minister that the surplus at the end of the period during which this step was in effect was infinitely greater than it was at the beginning.
It seems to me that if we are going to get rid of our butter surplus, some additional step will have to be taken. I may be alone in the house in taking such an attitude, but I think that the basic trouble with our butter policy at the moment is that the 58 cent floor price is too high. It is too high for the good of the consumer, it is too high for the good of the taxpayer, and it is too high for the good of the producer.
You are sure alone.

I know that originally the
58 cent floor price was introduced by the government in good faith, in an effort to help the producer, and in an effort to stabilize the dairy industry. Yet I contend that the legislation is having the opposite effect. As I stated a moment ago, about all that this subsidy has done is to force thousands and thousands of Canadians, who otherwise would probably be eating butter, into eating margarine and similar substitutes.
The statistics will bear out that fact and I should like to quote some from the dominion bureau of statistics. These show that in 1953 the per capita consumption of butter was 20-88 pounds, while in 1954 it had dropped to 20-69 pounds. In the same period the per capita consumption of margarine jumped from 7-45 pounds in 1953 to 7-61 pounds in 1954. As I see it, the Canadian butter producer is gradually losing his share of the Canadian market because of this artificial floor price.
Would the hon. member put on the record the cost of producing this butter?

I must tell the hon. member for Moose Mountain that I cannot put that cost on the record, but I could find it very easily, as could he. I will be ready to help him look it up later on if he wishes to.
What about the export market for butter? The export market for Canadian butter has completely disappeared. The reason is fairly obvious. It has disappeared because the world market price is about one-third lower

Supply-Agriculture
than the Canadian price. For instance, New Zealand today is laying down butter in Great Britain at under 40 cents a pound. Now, if the minister or the government should decide to try to get rid of our surplus butter by exporting it, the taxpayer is going to be called on for a very huge subsidy. If we sold 50 million or 60 million pounds at a competitive world price in the export market to dispose of our surplus, it might cost the taxpayer anywhere from $10 million up.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say this in order not to scare the taxpayer too much. There is no possibility of selling 50 million or 60 million pounds of butter out of Canada without running our own people short.

I should like to tell the minister that sooner or later he is going to have to take some action to get rid of his surplus butter. He does not want it to spoil on his hands. Each month that goes by, the surplus is getting larger as compared with the same period a year ago.

Mr. Chairman, if I may be permitted, I should like to say that the hon. gentleman was just criticizing the method by which that has been done for the last two years. We know that, if we were still holding 1953 butter, it might go bad, but we do not have any. We sold our older butter at 56 cents and got new butter in to replace it. That is the plan, under which we do know butter could not be spoiled.

I wish to sum up the present situation as I see it, rightly or wrongly. The Canadian butter producer has lost his export markets. Each month that goes by, he is being squeezed out of the domestic market. What should be done? The present government program has been costly to the taxpayer. I would not object to that, if it were actually helping the producer but, as I say, I am convinced that it has not. I think that both the government and the dairy industry must face certain hard, harsh economic facts. If the producer wishes to regain his share of the Canadian market, he is going to have to bring his prices down to a competitive level. I cannot see any other way around it. I believe in reasonable floor prices for agricultural products-but note that I say "reasonable". As far as butter is concerned, there is a complicating factor because of the substitutes which exist. The only way that this government can eventually deal with our mounting surpluses is to reduce floor prices by four or five cents a pound, to a point where they will be more competitive with margarine. I would remind 
you, Mr. Chairman, and the house, that a year ago President Eisenhower took precisely such action in the United States. He reduced the floor price of butter by a few cents, and immediately consumption increased by 7 per cent. So I say to you that this parliament should give serious consideration to revising our floor price structure on butter. I would say, by all means keep a floor price, but make that floor price more realistic.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on the minister's estimates, I wish to bring up again a subject I have brought up already. It is the most important subject in my constituency, as far as agriculture is concerned.
The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa has made it much easier for me because he has dealt with the flood situation in his constituency. I know what his problem is, because part of his constituency used to be mine. Now I have a worse situation than I ever had before, because we do not have good roads by means of which we can build dikes. The two lakes that enclose the interlake country are 4-7 feet above normal, and everything is flooded. Take the Fisher Branch, Broad Valley, Eriksdale, Riverton, and the St. Martin districts. There is just one lake running into another. The people in these districts had Selkirk wheat to sow, but they have given up the hope now because it is too late to sow it, and they will not be able to sow any crop. It is to be hoped that in July they may get some grain feed in.
The minister knows my problem because I have talked it over with him at different times, and I am hopeful he will be able to do something for these farmers. I do not know what the solution is. I do not know how much money the government can spend on it, but certainly something will have to be done to keep these people alive, so that we do not lose them. They had practically no crop last year, and they have not been able to sow anything this year. I tried to make some calls there at Eastertime, and I had to be pulled out with a tractor four times on the main road. With conditions like that, it is so hard to know what to do. The hay lines are flooded with water. The cows are going along picking branches and they are getting sore feet from walking through the water. Some of the people have put away their herds and have just kept some foundation. I do not know whether the suggestion made by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa would help, that we might take flooded areas into consideration, as the P.F.A.A. only applies to crop land at the present time, or to crop that has been destroyed. It would help some. I do not. know why the provincial government in

Manitoba has not made a survey and got in touch with the federal government on this matter, because it is so serious. I know that the minister is doing some work in conjunction with the provincial government, but I believe it is going to extend over five years. This is something that needs immediate attention. I can go on repeating myself about the terrible conditions of the people in the interlake country, but I do not know that it would do any good. I have made representations to the minister and I have brought it to the attention of other people. Relief of some kind will have to be given to these people. They cannot just lift up and go away. Some of the men folk may go away, but it is hard for these men folk to get jobs in the city of Winnipeg; jobs are not too plentiful there.
The hon. member for Acadia talked about crop insurance. That is all right, but even crop insurance at this time would not help the people in the interlake area. The Minister of Agriculture should have a survey made to see the deplorable conditions these people are in and see if something could be done for them. I could elaborate on this and tell you stories and read letters from the district, but I want you to take my word for it that there is nothing political about this. It would not matter who was representing the constituency of Selkirk; they would run up against the same problem. I appeal to the government most urgently to try to do something for these poor people. Some of them certainly can get by, but a big percentage of them will not be able to get through. I appeal to the minister and ask him to appeal in turn to the treasury benches to try to do something for these poor folks.

Mr. Chairman, on the first item of the department it is usual to have a general discussion on agricultural problems. This afternoon we have heard a considerable amount about flood conditions in Manitoba and we sympathize with the people affected. I first want to congratulate the hon. member for Middlesex East on his speech last night. If he considered that he was pinch-hitting for anyone, may I say that I am sure he did not need to apologize; he scored many hits.
I want to say a word with regard to this flooding situation. I want to reiterate what the hon. member for Middlesex East said last night, namely that we have never in any way criticized any of the grants or assistance given to the western farmer such as that under P.F.R.A. or P.F.A.A. But in the case of Ontario last fall as the result of "Hurricane Hazel" our losses were simply terrific. Millions and millions of dollars were lost in crops
Supply-Agriculture
that were never harvested. Corn along the Grand river that could not be harvested was a complete loss. Yet those farmers did not receive one nickel for that loss. It is true that the vegetable growers received some remuneration through the Hurricane Hazel relief fund which was mainly taken up by a collection of people in Ontario who realized the seriousness of the situation and gave freely of their own funds to help those people out. Certainly we received a grant from the dominion government of $1 million but that was probably about one-tenth of the loss that was sustained and for which moneys were paid out.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

I am quite interested in this matter. I was interested in that whole "Hurricane Hazel" matter. I wonder whether the Ontario people asked for more than the $1 million. Did they ask for a considerable sum and find it refused?
All the Ontario people asked for was a fair and reasonable amount of money to be given to them in this case of a national disaster.
Who decided on the $1 million?

The dominion government decided on it, apparently. This government here decided on that amount to be given to those people. But the damage was not only the result of "Hurricane Hazel"; it was the result of flooding caused by the extreme amount of rainfall which amounted in some districts to eight inches or nine inches over a period of 24 hours.
Again, Mr. Chairman, I want to say something about the planning of the debates in this House of Commons in relation to the sittings of the committee on agriculture and colonization. Here we are this afternoon debating the estimates of the Department of Agriculture-

I was attending a farmers' picnic in Haldi-mand county at which the lieutenant governor of the province of Ontario was a guest of honour and guest speaker. It was my honour and privilege to be in attendance at that picnic and to show my respect for the lieutenant governor of Ontario. Are there any other questions?
