speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Do not complain about not being here when the agricultural estimates are under discussion.

The agriculture estimates
were not under consideration yesterday. I am complaining about discussion of the agriculture estimates being held at the same time as the meetings of the committee on agriculture. I have complained about that matter several times but apparently it does not seem to do a particle of good. As I have said previously in the House of Commons and in the committee, the bill that was standing on the order paper from January 11 was called in the house on the very first day that the meeting of the committee on agriculture was called. That is just a sample of the planning of the business of this House of Commons that is carried on by this government.

On two previous occasions I tried to answer that complaint and my hon. friend interrupted me in the middle of it, with the result that I did not get back to it. I do not know why he rises now and states it all over again. It has no relationship to these estimates. The Department of Agriculture has not referred anything to the committee on agriculture. The committee on agriculture is sitting to consider a matter that was brought before it by the Department of Trade and Commerce. I have attended the committee on agriculture for only about 15 minutes during all the time they have been sitting. It has nothing to do with this department whatsoever.

If the minister thinks he
answered that complaint before, may I say that I did not hear his explanation.
I did not make it before because you did not let me make it.

I did not interrupt the
minister when he was making his speech. I have never interrupted the minister in any speech he has ever made in the House of Commons.
No. My hon. friend rose and asked me a question that got me off on something else and I did not get back to it.

Mr. Chairman, I am making a statement of fact and I do not think the minister can refute that fact. Whether it is under the Department of Trade and Commerce or not, it has to do with agricultural matters. Regardless of whether or not he thinks it is under a different department, it has to do with agricultural matters.
I have refuted the inference you are drawing. I am not refuting the facts you stated.
Order.

It still has to do with agricultural matters. It is dealing mainly with western agriculture or dealing with wheat. It is true it has to do with the matter of feed problems here in the east and we did discuss that matter to some extent. But I am still critical of his government for having had an occasion arise when the committee on agriculture was meeting at the same time and was called on the same day as one bill that had been standing on the order paper from January 11 was brought forward in the house. That is all I am going to say on that matter, but I think it is an example of extremely poor planning on the part of this government to let that be the fact.
With regard to the farmers' position today, I want to go back a little bit in history because apparently there is a good deal of confusion among people in urban areas as to farm thinking. I regret to say it but there are few people living in large cities in this country or in the United States who understand the farm psychology. They say that the farmer beefs a lot. They criticize him for getting money handed to him by way of subsidies and that sort of thing. But they do not understand what that farmer puts up with. They do not understand his way of life.
Years and years ago the farmer was in fact self-sufficient. He did not need to worry very much about what happened in the cities. He grew his own food. He made his own clothes. He made his own implements, as it were. He even made his own bullets with which to shoot the food he ate or part of it. But as time went along that condition changed. It changed considerably with the advent of an increased population in the country. One hundred years ago probably 90 per cent of the people in this country were on farms and depended on farms for a living, and the agricultural income was in proportion to the number of people getting their living from the farm. At that time the consumer in the city realized where his food came from. In most cases he dealt directly with the man who grew the food. He bought his potatoes, his fruit and his vegetables from the farmer himself. Today the farmer's position has changed in that he is no longer self-sufficient. He requires fuel to use in his tractor. He no longer uses horses for which he grew the necessary fuel. He has to purchase fertilizers, and in many cases he has to purchase feed. Therefore the farmer has placed himself in the position of being a consumer of a great many goods.

But the consumer in the urban districts is also in a different position. He has lost his personal contact with the producer of his food. Many young people in our cities hardly know what a farm is or what a cow looks like. I would even go so far as to say that many young people in our cities today probably wonder what colour of cow chocolate milk comes from. As a matter of fact, I have been asked that question by young people. The consumer now goes to the chain store. He purchases his food in packages, and very attractive packages they are. There is no definite link between the consumer and the man who produces the food. It is more or less an automatic process and I regret to say that many people in our cities take food for granted. There is good reason for that. Never in the history of the country has anybody ever gone hungry because of a scarcity of food. There has always been plenty, and often there have been surpluses. I regret to say, for that very reason many people take food for granted.
In his opening remarks the other night the minister made some statements about prices. I want to quote a paragraph from his speech to be found at the bottom of page 4210 of Hansard of May 27. He said:
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture statement points out that prices of farm products have fallen further in North America than in other countries of the world. This is quite true, but prices in general after the drop are higher in North America than in other countries of the world, all of which indicates that since the war farmers in North America have had the highest prices in the world.
I should also like to quote one sentence from the middle of a paragraph on the next page, and I do not think it is unfair to quote only the one sentence. The minister said:
The shrinkage of foreign markets, however, came about partly because there has been a higher price level here than elsewhere.
In the one case the minister says that our farm prices are the highest in the world, which is true, but later he qualifies that statement by saying that the shrinkage of foreign markets came about partly because there has been a higher price level here than elsewhere. Certainly the only thing that actually counts is the net income the farmer receives. As found on page 4212, the minister said:
No sound conclusion can be reached by comparing anything related to production or returns from farming, by comparing one year with the one before it or the one immediately after it.
Then the minister went on to say that the prices in any four-year period since the Liberals have formed the government have been higher than they ever were in the period from 1931 to 1934. We have heard that argument so often, Mr. Chairman. Does
S upply-A griculture
the government believe that the farmers of this country will accept that sort of statement? There was a world depression then and prices were down, but later in my speech I hope to show by figures that the situation in proportion to other prices was not as bad then as the government would like to lead people to believe.
Net farm income for 1954 was down by something like 48 per cent. In 1951 net farm income was $2,154 million, and in 1954 it was $1,125 million. The minister says that, taking the average of the last four years, prices have been better than they ever were before. I have here the April, 1955, issue of the Economic Annalist, and I want to give a few figures from this publication. Taking the period from 1935 to 1939 as representing 100, the average figure for farm prices for the five-year period from 1943 to 1947 is 188-9 while the figure for January, 1955, is 221-2. These figures are for farm prices of agricultural products.
Let us now take the composite index of commodity prices. The average of those prices for the same five-year period, 1943 to 1947, was 154-2, and by January, 1955, the figure had increased to 231 -7. What is interesting is the difference between the figures representing the five-year average from 1943 to 1947 inclusive and the figures for January, 1955. As far as farm prices are concerned, there has been an increase of 17 per cent between the average for the years 1943 to 1947 and the figure as at January, 1955. There is an increase of 17 per cent.
In which direction?

Up. I said "increase". As far as commodity prices are concerned, prices for the things the farmer has to buy, there has been an increase from 154-2 to 231-7, an increase of 77-5 or practically 50 per cent. There, Mr. Chairman, is your answer.
Is the last one a five-year average too?
No, of course the last one is not. I said I took the figure for January, 1955.
That just proves what I said is correct. It does not get you anywhere to compare five years with one day.
There is never any use in placing figures on Hansard as far as the Minister of Agriculture is concerned.
Not that kind of figure.

He places his own figures on Hansard to show his own trend of thought, but anybody else's figures do not mean a thing.

Supply-Agriculture
You are doing well.
I have taken these figures from the Economic Annalist, and I challenge the minister-
This is funny money.
Yours is sometimes, you mean.

The minister seems to be having a lot of fun. He does not bother me a bit, so let him have his fun. I say again, that is the answer to our problem today. The net income of the farmer is down 48 per cent, and that is the reason it is down. The prices of farm products have gone up only 17 per cent on an average over the five-year period 1943-47, while the commodities the farmer has to buy have gone up 50 per cent. The farmer's net income has been greatly decreased as is shown by these figures.
The minister went on to quote what the figures were back in the period 1931-34. This Economic Annalist, put out by the Department of Agriculture, does not include comparable figures for those years, so I have no way of proving anything by quoting figures from this pamphlet. In the column relating to farm prices of agricultural products there is, however, another item here, the general wholesale index for 1931-34. This index varies from 94 down to 86-9. I remind hon. members that these figures are all quoted on the basis of 1935-39 equalling 100. Then the composite index of commodities and services used by farmers for the period 193134, as compared with the high of 94 and the low of 86-9 for the general wholesale index, goes from a low of 89-8 to a high of 100-9. There is not as much difference there, Mr. Chairman, in the 1931-34 period as there is now in this 1955 period.
I should like to quote a paragraph from the minister's statement in Hansard of May 27, 1955, page 4212. He said:
I have before me a table which shows that, taking the average price on farm products for the 4 years before we came into office as the beginning, there has been an increase every 4 years since, until now the price on all cereals is from 2J to 3 times as high from 1951 to 1954 as in 1931 to 1934.
Just imagine, 2J times to 3 times as much.
The price on hogs is over 3 times as high, and the price on cattle over 4 times as high. The price on butter is 2i times as high, the price on cheese 3 times as high and the price on eggs almost twice as high.
Now, is that not something to be proud of? The minister compared the average prices in 1931-34 with the average prices in 1951-54, after we have had a war, and conditions have changed so much. Our economy has entirely changed, and our dollar is worth

just half as much, and yet the minister insists on comparing these two periods.
I put a table on Hansard of March 15 that appears at page 2066. This table showed quite clearly that there never has been a year in the history of this country when an hour's wages would buy so much food. That, Mr. Chairman, is the answer to the farmers' problem and the answer to many other problems across this country, especially the unemployment problem. If any other industry or any other class of people were asked to take a 48 per cent net decrease in income in the last four years, I wonder what would happen. But the farmer, has taken a 48 per cent decrease in net income, and people wonder why there is unemployment in this country. The implement manufacturers are practically closed down because they cannot sell their implements. The farmers have not the dollars to buy these implements. Yet, the minister gets up and says they are better off than they ever were before.
May I ask my hon. friend how long * this government would stay in office if we put conditions back to what they were from 1931 to 1935? We would go out as fast as your party went out.
It was a Liberal government that put them there in the first place, because that depression started long before 1930 and the minister knows it very well.
Why did you not say that from the start instead of arguing the other way?
I have listened to the minister now for quite a number of years and I am getting used to him. As a matter of fact, I do not pay too much attention to what he says on many occasions.
Some people do.

But that is a fact; it is here in Hansard. The minister says that farmers are better off now than they ever were. I am just going to leave it to the farmers themselves to say whether or not they are better off than they ever were. They will probably say it in another way at the next election.
You have been making that prophecy ever since you came here.
Sometimes it takes quite a while for things to seep in, you know, but the farmers are getting just about as fed up as I have ever seen them. I think probably the minister knows that very well.
That is why he is on edge.
I am not on edge.

We hear a great deal, Mr. Chairman, about the subsidies paid to farmers. This afternoon we listened to a speech by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. He has his own ideas, and he is entitled to them. I am sorry he is not in the house now but I do want to say to him that, although I cannot quote the exact figure for the subsidy on butter, the amount is infinitesimal. The amount that'subsidy costs the taxpayers of this country is infinitesimal. I must be fair, however, and say that the farmers of the country do appreciate the fact the government kept the floor price at 58 cents. The government showed very good judgment in doing so. They knew what would happen under the circumstances if they had lowered that floor price, on top of the importation of 2-25 million pounds of New Zealand cheese. The farmers of this country were up in arms just a little farther than I have ever seen them in my life before as a result of that importation. As I say, I have to be fair to the minister, and the farmers do appreciate the maintenance of that floor price.
It has been suggested that the farmers should be able to compete in the free market of the world and left to themselves to go along in the best way they can, without any support prices and without any floor prices. I will say that in most things the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre is consistent, although I wonder if he would like to see everything thrown wide open. I think the farmers of this country would take their chance if that were the case, but when one industry has protection they believe they are entitled to some protection at least.
It was stated also that the floor price did not help the producer. I cannot conceive of anyone making that statement. I will say this, Mr. Chairman, that the maintenance of the floor price on butter helps the consumer just as much as it does the producer. It stops these great fluctuations in price. I will say that during the period from 1947 to 1953 inclusive the total subsidies paid to agriculture, including the subsidy of $69 million paid out for losses as a result of foot-and-mouth disease, amounted to less than 15 cents per capita per year.
It is true that in 1952 there was an increase in the price of butter. It was unnecessary, and of course it stayed up for only a day or so, because when it was found that stocks were not as low as some people had led us to believe, the price broke. I think it dropped as much as 17 or 18 cents in one day.
I wish to point out that by maintaining the floor price on butter the consumers of this country are assured that they will not have to pay an extremely high price for their
Supply-Agriculture
butter in the wintertime, even though they might get it at a low price in the summer. The cost of the subsidy has been saved many times over through the maintenance of stability and farmer purchasing power.
A number of years ago the farmers of this country were promised that if they would accept lower prices during the war they would receive a square deal after the war was over. Let me quote what was said in this connection in a radio broadcast by the former prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, on December 4, 1943, he said:
If, to help win the war, the farmers are asked to accept a ceiling on prices, we believe they are entitled to a floor under prices to insure them against an agricultural depression after the war.
The farmers were also promised that markets in Great Britain would be retained if they accepted lower than the world price during the war. But what happened? Practically all those markets were lost. I mentioned a moment ago that subsidies have been criticized from many quarters.
I should like to put on the record some figures concerning other subsidies-and these are not paid to farmers. I have before me the answer to a question appearing in Hansard of May 4. On that date the hon. member for Jasper-Edson asked the following question:
What was the total amount paid in price support of gold mining industry in 1954?
To that question the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys replied:
Assistance paid by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys during the calendar year 1954 amounted to $14,879,334.33.
Strangely enough immediately following this question was another asked, again, by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson. His second question was:
What was the total amount paid for price support on all farm commodities in 1954?
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture replied as follows:
The estimated net cost of operations of the agricultural prices support board during the 195455 fiscal year ending March 31, 1955, is $3,210,928.
In other words about four and a half times as much was paid by way of subsidies to the gold mining industry in this country, which employs approximately 25,000, as was paid to agriculture in which 660,000 are employed. I place these figures on record at this time to point out to the people of Canada that farmers are not the only ones who are receiving subsidies. It is costing the taxpayers of this country very little for the help being given to the farmers. As I said before it amounted to 15 cents per capita per year over a six-year period.
It is claimed that prices are high. I said a few moments ago that there never has
I did not say that at any time in my life. I never have said the farmers were well off.

Perhaps the minister did
not say so, but-
I am a farmer, myself, and I know.
Then we will have to presume that they are not well off, and he is now admitting it.
Better off than they were under the Tories.

The minister says that they are better off than they ever were before. The government has a long way to go to make it possible for the farmers to say that they are well off. And the minister admits that they are not well off.
They have been getting along so well as compared with the way they got along under other governments that they are content to keep us here.
There are no fishermen going to California, I can tell you that.

I would like to put a few
more figures on record.
Could we call it six o'clock?
May I ask what we shall be discussing after eight o'clock?
We will continue with these estimates.

I think I ought to say to hon. members who asked me last night to try not to go on tonight that we have tried to make arrangements, which we could not, to have others do so. That was impossible for certain reasons, not all originating on this side of the house, and for that reason I will go on tonight.

In view of the social engagements which Saskatchewan members have, as acting leader it is my intention to ask for the adjournment of the house at a quarter to ten this evening so that they may attend the Saskatchewan functions.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, I hope I may be permitted to tell the minister that during the recess tonight we were very much impressed by the group of young men and young women coming from his own province, carrying the banner of the Saskatchewan golden jubilee and representing the high schools of the prairie province.
Before six o'clock I was very sorry to hear the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand making a comparison between the subsidies paid by the federal government to the agricultural industry on one hand and those paid to the gold-mining industry on the other, for the simple reason that a great part of the gold subsidy is benefiting the farmers of northern Ontario and northern Quebec. I would be very much afraid to think of what would become of our farmers if the goldmining industry was closed down. The gold subsidy is one way of helping the farmers, and there should be no suggestion of discontinuing it at this time.

I shall be brief in my remarks, Mr. Chairman. First I wish to congratulate the minister on his comprehensive statement on the general situation in Canadian agriculture at the present time.
I also wish to offer my sincere thanks to the officers and the technicians of the department for all they have done to help the farmers of our district. More particularly, I wish to say that the farmers of northwestern Quebec are grateful to the directors, the technicians and the other employees of the federal experimental farm of Kapuskasing and of the experimental substation of 'Maca-mic for their guidance, and the good advice and encouragement they have supplied in performing their duty. We are in great need of this kind of service and we hope that it will be accelerated.
Agriculture gradually becomes a basic industry in northwestern Quebec, more particularly within the clay belt which is eminently suited to the production of fodder plants, and consequently to stock farming, either for meat or for dairy products. Also, small-scale farming and gardening can be made profitable around the larger centres such as Rouyn-Noranda, Malartic, Val d'Or-Bour-lamaque and Amos. In this respect, I would hope that the division of horticulture of Kapuskasing would conduct some experimental work in the growing and preparation for market of vegetables in those centres. There are a great number of small farms which are suitable for that kind of production, and their owners are in urgent need of guidance and encouragement. I will go as far as saying that an experimental station for that purpose would be a profitable investment.
As it is, in northwestern Quebec, the development of agriculture depends mostly on the mining industry. The latter injects a pecuniary serum, enabling the settler to live through the difficult years when he has to work on virgin soil which will bear fruits only after years of unceasing labour. The settler finds in the mining centres a ready market for his lumber and other farm products, and the mining industry provides work for him during the off-season. So, gradually, the settlement lot becomes a productive farm, and the settler a real farmer ready to take his rightful place in the community.
Now, the majority of our farmers are at a stage where they need more help, additional guidance and encouragement. They need help in connection with their livestock and in connection with the classification, storage and distribution of their products. Studies of these various problems are now being made by local organizations, but it is only with
Supply-Agriculture
the help of duly qualified technicians, the guidance of good management, the encouragement of the business people of our district and the financial aid from both the federal and provincial governments that a program of such breadth can be carried out.
There are over 65,000 people in the cities and towns of northwestern Quebec. Carloads of such commodities as meat, vegetables, dairy products and poultry come from outside the district and are distributed by many merchants in the different localities. In such a situation we would think that the local products would find an outlet. We are aware of the fact, however, that a grocer cannot buy products that are not classified. Moreover, if he is not assured of a steady flow of products from the local farmers, he cannot buy from them. Our farmers need a distribution centre in which they can find facilities such as a slaughter house, cold storage and good management for the distribution of their products. These facilities are lacking at present, so the flow of products is not steady. This is partly due to a lack of guidance in distribution. Further progress could be made also by a livestock improvement program, jointly operated with a program for the development of grasses. This would enable the farmers of the district to continue the production of livestock on a more sustained basis.
Finally-and I have mentioned this before- so that the farming industry in northwestern Quebec may fulfil expectations, let us hope that a large-scale program of drainage will be undertaken with the co-operation of both federal and provincial governments in the whole of this part of the Pre-Cambrian clay belt, which is level with the farm lands. In addition to improving arable land, it would help reforestation and the development of large marshlands which are now absolutely useless.
The farmers of northwestern Quebec keep toiling to clear and improve their farms. The heavy work they took on from the beginning is now producing results. However, if we want the progress of the farmers of our district to be on a par with that of other industries, we will have to give a hand, we will have to help those who have worked so hard to clear the land and, finally, we will have to try to make it easier for the farmers to distribute their products. We know how steadfast our farmers are, and if we help them ever so little we may be sure that they will do their full share in the development and progress of that part of the country.

Mr. Chairman, last week in the committee on broadcasting we were

Supply-Agriculture
privileged to hear representatives from the musicians union. The suggestion was put forward by that group that it might be a good idea if members of the House of Commons organized some sort of musical group in order to increase harmony in the chamber.
We have one on this side of the house.

After hearing the excellent performance by the western young people during the supper recess, I am sure that we would all agree that the union representatives had a worth-while suggestion to make for members of the house. Already tonight I think the discussion on agricultural subjects is proceeding on a more harmonious note than before the commencement of the recess. In my contribution I hope to continue on that same level as far as is possible.
I was delighted this afternoon to hear the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa take up the cudgels in no uncertain terms in behalf of the proposed Russell reservoir. I say that I was delighted to hear him take this stand because hitherto the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa has rather inclined to the view that diking instead of the reservoir was the solution for the problem of flooding in the Manitoba area.
I have been interested in this subject ever since I came into the house. Each year since the report was prepared by P.F.R.A. on the problem of flooding on the Assiniboine river I have asked the Minister of Agriculture on the estimates when action might be contemplated on the basis of the report. Last year, unfortunately, the minister was not able to be in the chamber during the discussion of the estimates. I therefore presented the question to his parliamentary assistant who was acting on his behalf. As reported at page 6738 of Hansard for 1954, I put this question to the parliamentary assistant:
Last year when I questioned the Minister of Agriculture on the matter he referred me to a report on conservation and flood control on the Assiniboine river that was prepared by the P.F.R.A. branch, and completed and published in December, 1952 . . . The report to which I have referred recommends two major projects in flood control and conservation in the Assiniboine basin. I refer to the Russell reservoir at Russell, Manitoba, and the Portage la Prairie diversion ... As I indicated, the minister said last spring when we were considering the estimates that the matter was under consideration. As this condition has been developing from 1886, and has been under consideration since that time, I would hope this year that some specific information might be available as to what the department contemplates in regard to the recommendations of the report.
In reply to that question, Mr. Chairman, as reported at page 6750 I finally succeeded in

getting from the parliamentary assistant, after I had queried him further, an answer as follows:
I understand that was with respect to the survey made of the Assiniboine river. That survey was undertaken along with the Red river survey at a time when they had flood trouble in the Red river valley a few years ago. These few projects were undertaken together but what is going to take place with respect to the survey in which my hon. friend is interested, X am not in a position to say.
I repeat the question this evening, Mr. Chairman, because it is becoming quite obvious that the problem on the Assiniboine river requires urgent attention on the part of the federal administration in co-operation with the other government levels concerned.
The reason I think the emphasis is being placed on the effectiveness of the Russell reservoir project today is the formation of the Assiniboine river control association last fall. It was my privilege to attend the organization meeting of this group made up of representatives from all the municipalities adjoining the Assiniboine river. At that time they spent several hours considering the three alternatives that have been proposed in solving this problem, namely, the reservoir; second, continuation of the program of diking; and third, the Portage diversionary cut-off into lake Manitoba. Even as far back as last fall members of the association came to the conclusion that neither diking nor the Portage diversion was the suitable solution and began to press for the Russell reservoir. Just two weeks ago they had another meeting to which the Minister of Agriculture was invited. At that meeting some further strong recommendations were forthcoming supporting the reservoir solution to the problem. Some of these resolutions were placed on record by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa this afternoon.
While the association has moved towards solid support for the reservoir, it has not entirely abandoned the principle of diking. It suggests, however, that diking is only a temporary solution to this flooding difficulty. The correctness of that suggestion definitely has been demonstrated by recent events in the district of Portage la Prairie. It will be recalled by hon. members that the city of Brandon was in the headlines, both in the press and on the radio, for a period of almost two weeks recently because in that city a heroic struggle was taking place to maintain their diking system intact. I am pleased to be able to say that largely as a result of action on the part of the municipal authorities, assisted by an excellent civil defence group supported by police and fire departments, Brandon was able to maintain its diking system intact and that no major

flood damage took place within the city proper. However, while Brandon was saved, the dikes erected there merely succeeded in pushing the additional water in the direction of Portage la Prairie and, as has already been indicated, the Portage dikes were breached and considerable damage done to the extremely fertile farm land of the Portage plains.
In reference to this diking problem I would further point out that the city of Brandon has spent in the past two years some $70,000 of its own funds. Of course I think it will be understood that an expenditure of that kind to cope with the flood problem is much too high for any one municipality to bear. I would therefore join heartily with the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa in suggesting that some definite action be taken with reference to the recommendations of the P.F.R.A. report on flooding on the Assiniboine river published in 1952 and that this action be taken in consultation with the municipal authorities as well as the provincial authorities.
Just before leaving the subject of flooding, which comes under the general heading of P.F.R.A. and P.F.A.A., I want to say I have received certain resolutions from municipalities and areas affected suggesting that something be done by way of compensating farmers who have been flooded out, in some cases for three years in succession. There is a group of farmers along the Assiniboine river in Saskatchewan as well as in Manitoba west of Brandon who have suffered almost complete crop failure during the past three years because of the regular flooding. Unfortunately, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Acadia, there is just no way under the P.F.A.A. scheme whereby these farmers can be compensated.
I know the government is aware of the problem because two or three weeks ago I submitted a motion for the tabling of letters, documents, etc., relating to the problem of flooding on the Assiniboine, and I have been informed by the government departments concerned that the correspondence is so voluminous they hardly know where to begin in responding to my motion. Obviously the government is well aware that the farmers of Manitoba are quite exercised over this difficulty. They are and have been so exercised that in the past year the provincial government established a committee to examine thoroughly the question of crop insurance. This of course is related to the whole problem of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and its adequacy in meeting present-day problems in the prairie provinces. While the committee has not yet submitted its final report
Supply-Agriculture
there is every indication through preliminary press releases that the consensus will be that the present P.F.A.A. legislation is quite inadequate to deal with the problems of floods and other agricultural hazards as they apply to the province of Manitoba.
From time to time farmers in Manitoba have complained because it was becoming increasingly obvious that Manitoba farmers were not receiving proportionate returns from their contributions to the P.F.A.A. scheme, largely because Manitoba does not have so much submarginal agricultural land as the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Even this year the figures for P.F.A.A. assistance, if I remember them correctly, are something like $19 million for Saskatchewan and $3 million for Manitoba. In addition, I have already had letters from farm constituents pointing out that any assistance they have been able to obtain under P.F.A.A. as it stands is quite inadequate to deal with the problem created largely by the flood emergency.
I am not going to take the time of the house tonight to deal with the question of crop insurance as comprehensively as did the hon. member for Acadia. That would merely be going over ground already covered. I would, however, point out very emphatically that Manitoba farmers are very much exercised over this matter, and no doubt when the report of the committee investigating crop insurance is brought down there will be strong recommendations that something be done to provide more adequate protection on an actuarially sound insurance basis not only for Manitoba farmers but for other farmers of the prairie section of Canada.
There is one final point, perhaps an incidental one, on the question of flooding to which I should like to refer before leaving this section of my remarks. I wish to draw the attention of the house to a report that emerged from a government department a few weeks ago concerning moisture control experiments that have been taking place in southwestern Manitoba and in two areas of west central Saskatchewan during the past two years. The Canadian Press report on the matter emanating from the government weather service branded as a failure the commercial rain-making experiments carried out in 1953 and 1954 in sections of the prairie wheat belt. The official summary of the weather service report says that the most likely effect of the cloud seeding was a decrease in rainfall of 14.1 per cent.
Since this official statement was made by this government source the group carrying

Supply-Agriculture
on these experiments in Manitoba and Saskatchewan have issued a counteracting statement in which they point out that the appraisal of the experiments is completely inadequate, if not entirely wrong or distorted, because no final opinion concerning the rain-making experiments can be formed until there have been at least seven years of experimentation in this particular section of the country. I am taking the opportunity tonight to point out that there has been considerable interest in this experiment among the farmers. Earlier in my remarks I talked about flooding, but most hon. members will recall that an excess of water is not the only problem of the prairie region. For many years during the so-called dirty thirties we had the problem of drought to contend with. This work relating to the drought problem has been carried out on a voluntary subscription basis by the farmers interested, and it is unfortunate that the government weather service allowed a premature report to be circulated before the scheme had had an opportunity to prove itself one way or the other.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni also dealt with this subject in the house on the 17th of May, and as found at page 3869 of Hansard for that day he stated:
As I stated somewhat facetiously, I admit, in conversation with some of my colleagues, if this situation were permitted to develop it is conceivable that we in British Columbia would have the power to turn the entire prairie provinces into a desert by taking all the water out of the clouds coming in from the Pacific.
The hon. member was. referring to similar experiments that have been taking place west of the mountains. He himself described his remarks as being somewhat facetious, but unfortunately the press picked up the statement I have quoted and headlined it in the west. They said that a member of parliament had .suggested the possibility that the prairies might become a desert as the result of cloud seeding weather modification experiments being carried out on Vancouver island. That, I trust, will put the record straight. I have taken the time of the house to do so because this publicity has been somewhat disturbing to the farmers who have invested substantial sums in this experiment.
Now before concluding, Mr. Chairman, I should like to have a brief word on general agricultural matters. This is the first time I have taken part in any agricultural debate in this chamber during the present session. There has been a great deal of time consumed in discussing the agricultural picture. Because it is in the process of transition, I have waited until we had the opportunity of hearing statements from the responsible

cabinet ministers, and particularly until we had the opportunity of getting the picture from the farm organizations, the representatives of the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners who appeared before the agriculture committee. The pattern that has been taking shape during the year has definitely come into focus during recent weeks.
I admit that the minister, in his general preamble to this discussion a week ago tonight, was very optimistic in his generalizations. I would conclude from his remarks, to use a phrase that might appropriately be used by one who is an Indian chief as well as a minister of the crown, that he believes all the smoke that has been raised in this chamber is, "heap big smoke and no fire". However, the Minister of Finance, in his budget speech, emphasized that agriculture was having a difficult time. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is also an optimist, made the announcement of the final payments for western grain and said he was disappointed in the final price which was the result of strong competitive factors in the export market, particularly competition arising from the United States surplus disposal program. There is, therefore, definitely some cause for alarm on the part of those who are vitally interested in the prairie agricultural economy.
The current review of agricultural conditions for Canada gives the farm net income for Canada by provinces for 1953 and 1954. I was interested to note that every province with the exception of the four western provinces pretty well maintained its net income position as between 1953 and 1954. On the other hand, Manitoba net income for 1953 was $110-6 million and for 1954 was $72-5 million, a percentage change of minus 34. The percentage change for those two years in Saskatchewan was minus 73, and the percentage change in Alberta was minus 42. I put that on the record, Mr. Chairman, merely to suggest that things are not too rosy in the prairie agricultural picture at least.
This fact was verified-
May I suggest that that verifies every statement I have made here in the last six months.
I do not quite understand that, Mr. Chairman.
Every time I have spoken on this question I have pointed out that the reduction in farm income in 1954 was brought about by what happened in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
I get the point.
Not altogether.
I am speaking largely from the viewpoint of the westerner, and therefore I stressed the prairie position.
I do, too.
That is obvious.

The appearance of the interprovincial farm union before the committee again indicated that they were very unhappy with the prairie agriculture position. I was most interested in one statement on page 4 of their brief to this effect:
For many years Canadian farmers advocated complete free trade, and if given that offered to produce in competition with all the world. This offer was spurned by Canadian industry which insisted on protection. Since that is now the accepted policy of Canada, we contend that Canadian farmers are entitled to equivalent benefits in some effective form.
I stress that phrase, "since that is now the accepted policy of Canada". I think that is the first time I have ever seen any western farm group appreciate the fact that the free trade propaganda that has been promulgated by a Liberal administration at Ottawa during the past two decades is a myth. They are now aware that Canada has a protectionist economy which favours the industrial provinces of central Canada. I think that is most significant. So far as I am concerned, it is the first time I have seen that expression of opinion from a prairie farm group.
The farmers' union opinion, as I understand it, is merely a new expression of the agricultural discontent that is peculiar to the prairies, and has been peculiar to the prairies ever since the early part of this century. It is the old agrarian protest raising its head again, a protest that has had such dramatic effect on Canadian social, political and economic life. But it is expressing itself in a somewhat different form this time, and definitely demonstrates that it has seen through the myth of the so-called Liberal free trade.
I have not much time left, but I want to say that the one observation that kept coming to my mind as I listened to the proceedings in the agriculture committee was this: After 20 years of continuous Liberal administration in Ottawa the prairie economy is still in a vulnerable position. We are still beset by the crisis of price and market, and this has been eloquently demonstrated in the remarks made by the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the various groups before the agriculture committee. In fact, if it were not for the existence of the wheat board the situation would be much more difficult than it actually is. If I might be allowed to say so, Mr. Chairman, I would
Supply-Agriculture
remind hon. members that the Canadian wheat board principle was laid down by a Conservative administration in 1935. There are many historical references in this chamber from time to time, and I am amazed at the tendency in all parts of the house towards the distortion of history.
I am reminded of a criticism that was once directed at Hitler and his henchmen when they were playing with history a few years ago in the greater Reich. Someone dared to criticize that gentleman to the effect that in the long run history would catch up with him; history would tell the true story. Hitler replied that he did not have the slightest misgiving in that regard because they would be writing history. I am afraid it is the tendency for all politicians to write history according to their own lights. I merely indicate that the wheat board principle, which emerged as a result of the economic crises of the thirties, was a by-product of a Conservative administration.
I would like to emphasize further, Mr. Chairman-because this point was discussed to a certain extent this afternoon-that, in turn, the depression of the thirties was a by-product of a century that had been saturated by what economists call Liberal laissez-faire economics. It was Mr. Bennett, with his new deal, and with his central bank principle, that first put a halt to the rather illusory and fanciful principles underlying Liberal laissez-faire economics which had dominated the western world ever since the industrial revolution.
I think that fact should be placed on the record, because sometimes even opposition groups are taken in by distortions of history, emanating from government sources. Just a short time ago the hon. member for Peace River, referring to the same period, suggested that Mr. Bennett had done nothing during the thirties to solve the problem. This is what he said, as it is reported at page 3986 of Hansard for May 20:
Every time anybody said to the Conservative government, "Why don't you get some purchasing power in circulation to start the wheels of industry going again?" the answer he got was, "There is not any money." They kept on saying that all through their regime up to 1935 when they were pitched out by the people of Canada largely because they had not found a solution or begun to find a solution for the unemployment problem.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I hope the hon. member will not continue to read into this debate the record of another debate on a different subject. I am sure he will agree with me when I suggest that if we are going to go into matters of history, other than those connected with agriculture, we will be a very long time disposing of the estimates of this

Supply-Agriculture
department. I would ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the estimates of this department.

I accept your gentle reprimand, Mr. Chairman, and shall conclude by saying that the significant and shocking fact that emerges from the recent discussion of agricultural problems is the fact that we in the west are just as vulnerable, just as unstable and just as economically immature as we were 20 years ago when a Liberal administration first took over. We will have these problems with us, and we will be wrestling with them until such time as we are able to establish a diversified and mature economy, not only in the two central provinces but right across the country. And I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that is the alternative the Conservative opposition has been offering for several years now-the development of national resources, both human and natural, so that we might deal with the basic and fundamental difficulties of the western economy.

Mr. Chairman, we in this group are not only concerned, but we are disappointed that at this session of parliament the government has failed to appreciate the very serious decline in Canada's agricultural position. We feel that at this session the government should have introduced some comprehensive farm program that would have placed agriculture back on a sound economic base.
In order to do this we believe that the new program should take into consideration a completely new approach to the problems agriculture is now facing. We believe that is necessary, if agriculture is going to make that contribution to the Canadian prosperity of which it is capable. And so it is because of these things I rise this evening to speak in criticism of the present agricultural policy the government is pursuing and has pursued in the past.
Certainly it is not my intention to place once again on the pages of Hansard the many arguments that have proved our contention that agriculture is in a difficult position. That has been done on numerous occasions, and was done again very well this afternoon by the hon. member for Mackenzie. However, in spite of the fact that many members on the opposition side of the house try to set out the problem faced by this industry in Canada, during the budget debate the Minister of Finance pointed out that in 1954 Canada's gross national product had fallen to the extent of some $400 million, and that in large measure, as a matter of fact to the extent of three-quarters, that drop was due
[The Deputy Chairman.]
to the fall in the income of farmers. On that admission therefore we can safely say that agriculture does play a tremendous part in the economy of the country.
It would be equally difficult to argue that the economic recession we see all across this country is not largely attributable to the very serious position in which agriculture finds itself today. Certainly the great measure of unemployment experienced throughout the country can be traced to the very unfavourable position of agriculture. That unemployment to a great extent has come about through lack of operations in the farm machinery industry, an industry which must be associated with agriculture; and the condition of that industry is due to the lack of purchasing power in the hands of Canadian agricultural producers.
Surely this condition has many repercussions. Figures from the dominion bureau of statistics show that in the last six months there has been a decline in retail sales in this country to the extent of $129 million. Businessmen throughout the country are holding meetings among themselves to try to devise some method whereby they will be able to continue in a liquid position, and still be able to supply in some measure the goods and services required by the agricultural producers. I am sure these men, not only in western Canada but in all parts of the country, have come to realize that we cannot let the farmer slide down the economic rat hole without its having very disastrous results on their own businesses. No wonder these businessmen are worried. When we look at the economic picture in agriculture we find that, in spite of the fact that we have experienced at least 10 years of good crops and high production, the agricultural policy being pursued by the government must stand condemned. In spite of this tremendous production in Canada farmers are experiencing a serious decline in purchasing power. I think it is a rather different situation. The farmers of western Canada have experienced five normal crops in so far as production is concerned in three years. It does not seem reasonable to me, when a condition like that has existed and one crop failure follows, that the farmer should find himself in a most embarrassing economic position. I think that there must be something wrong with the agricultural industry of this country when it is not able to survive one crop failure after having harvested five normal crops in the three years previous.
This afternoon the hon. member for Acadia spoke in support of crop insurance. Apparently he has given a great deal of study to

this matter because he spoke at length and in detail. It is not my intention to discredit anything he said, as I think this is a question that needs considerable study. Personally I have reservations as to the merits of a comprehensive crop insurance plan that will do the job.
I believe that subsidies of any kind are not going to provide an answer to the agricultural program. I believe that agriculture, like any other industry, should stand on its own feet. I believe it could do that and we would be able to eliminate many of the subsidies now being paid, and which are not doing the job, if we had an agricultural program that gave the farmer a return that had some relationship to his cost of production.
The average net income of Canadian farmers is in the neighbourhood of $2,000 per year. Agricultural producers feel that they should have an income not less than that of workers in non-agricultural industries. As I mentioned before, when we say that, we do not mean that the non-agricultural workers should get less, but we do contend that the agricultural workers should get more.
With the average income of Canadian farmers being in the neighbourhood of $2,000, that means that a great many farmers in this country are getting less than $2,000. I submit that that is rural poverty with a vengeance. We contend that agriculture should get its fair share of the national income. I am aware that arguments are made that that can never happen. We are told that agriculture must become more efficient; that you cannot expect the national income to be shared among farmers who are not efficient. I agree with that to some extent, but I think this talk of inefficiency in agriculture is overdone. I believe that this talk of efficiency in industry is overdone. I doubt very much if industry is as efficient as we are led to believe. So I do not think we should take that kind of argument into consideration when we ask that the farmer get a fair share of the national income.
This afternoon the hon. member for Mackenzie placed on the record the fact that while some 14 per cent of the people of Canada are engaged actively in agriculture they get only about 8-7 per cent of the national income. The farmer's position has deteriorated over the last 20 years and it has deteriorated very quickly over the last three years.
I should like to place on the record one set of figures to substantiate my argument that last year the farm net income declined by 30 per cent according to the figures of the dominion bureau of statistics. In 1953 net farm 50433-279
Supp ly-A griculture
income in this country was $1,669,600,000, yet in 1954 that net farm income had declined to $1,125,600,000. In all probability it will be even lower this year. During the last three years the net farm income of agricultural producers has fallen by 50 per cent but on the other hand operating costs have remained constant or have declined only slightly. As a matter of fact in 1954 they declined by only 2 per cent. For the three-year period to which I just referred in which farm net income declined by 50 per cent the cost of production dropped by only 5 per cent.
I think it is common knowledge that when farm production in respect to grain and livestock falls by as little as 5 per cent, farm prices fall by as much as 20, 30 or 40 per cent. Again, when the demand for some particular farm product drops off by 5 per cent farm prices fall, not by 5 per cent but by 10, 20 or 25 per cent.
This price squeeze, this disparity between the prices received by the farmers for what they produce and the cost of production, bears no relationship. This is the thing which is causing great concern today to the industry. There is no relationship between the prices the farmer gets and costs involved in his production. Under the present economic setup today agricultural producers are trying to operate when their costs are administered. Not only is the farmer open to all the hazards of farming, he must deal with things beyond his control outside of these administered costs. He seems to be legitimate prey for everyone.
As someone has said before, and I think this is significant, the farmer is the only person who sells at wholesale and buys at retail. As was said by an hon. member this afternoon, farm prices have changed most radically over the last 25 years. Mechanization is costly and because of the tremendous mechanization that is taking place in agriculture the farmer must have a greater return to support it.
The government is concerned over surplus production of wheat and many people in the government are advocating that production should be cut in the hope that prices will be maintained. I admit that that is a policy which can be carried on most effectively in industry where you can maintain prices by cutting production, but the very opposite is true with respect to agriculture. As soon as prices fall, the agricultural producer, in order to maintain his income, increases his production. That has been the story in Canada over and over again. We believe that the time is overdue when we must have some new approach, if we are

Supply-Agriculture
going to solve this problem with which we are faced. As I said a moment ago, I believe it is impossible to hope that subsidies are going to do the job; I do not believe they will. Subsidies should not have to be used. I believe that, if there were some relationship between farmers' prices and their costs, we would not need many of the subsidies which we are using today; but until that happens we have no alternative but to continue to ask for subsidies and to expand them.
In connection with this question, I should like to ask the minister something concerning P.F.A.A. Certainly I do not look on that as a subsidy in the same way as I did the other matters I mentioned, but it is rather unfair that, in certain parts of the country where farmers had a crop failure last year and have no prospect of a crop this year, they are being denied P.F.A.A. payments because they are forced to take some part-time employment in order to keep their families. I hope some leniency will be shown in some of those cases. I can very well understand the overall policy and I see nothing wrong with it, because we all know that a great many people living in every town in Canada own land. Certainly sometimes it is only a part-time occupation, but I feel that, because of the crop failure that was experienced in most of western Canada last year, where a farmer went out in the winter months and took parttime work, even when he knew he was not going to harvest a crop, some consideration should be given in those cases.
We believe that, if we are to evolve a farm production that will do the job, it should be based on the parity concept where we would have some relationship between prices and costs. In advocating such a policy, we believe we are completely justified. This is nothing new. I will admit that the Americans are in trouble to some extent in some phases of their parity scheme, but in the main much of that could have been avoided if some different administration had been used in that policy. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture and other important farming bodies of this country are supporting the principle of parity. Whilst the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is advocating a sliding scale, I cannot accept that. Parity means equality; it means justice; and if anybody can tell me that there is such a thing as 70 or 75 per cent of justice, then I have something to learn. You cannot have 75 per cent of justice. You either have full justice or you do not have any justice.	So I
maintain that we in this country must advocate full parity. When I say "full parity", I do not mean full parity on everything


across the board. I do not think that is necessary; I think it would be disastrous. I do not mean that at all. We should establish a system of parity prices. We should establish the principle of parity. I cannot think of any other industry or any other business in this country that operates on any other basis than that they have some regard for what the product is going to cost them. If they do not take that into consideration, they are just not in business. Yet the farmer goes on year after year in the hope that he will get back the cost of his production, and he very seldom has. We believe that agriculture is important enough in Canada's economy to warrant our . asking that it should receive the same consideration as that enjoyed by every other industry in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I can assure the house and tha minister that I have no intention of delaying him. I understand that the Saskatchewan concert meeting down town is waiting for the highlight of the evening, that is for the Minister of Agriculture to open the meeting. Judging from the rate at which we are going now, he will not get there in time to pronounce the benediction. I wish to deal tonight with one point in particular, and that is the price support on butter. I am strongly in favour of all sound price support schemes. When I think of all the price support schemes we have had in Canada so far, I believe the price support on butter is the soundest. For one thing, as a city man, I am strongly in favour of maintaining the farmer's income by any reasonable and sound method; and I believe this is a sound method.
But I want to point out that there are two sides to a pound of butter. If you have price supports which keep the income from butter high enough to enable the farmer to make a living, perhaps at times you make the price of butter so high that some people who should be able to eat butter cannot afford to eat butter at all and have to eat that unspeakably poor substitute for butter, namely margarine, which I am sure is having a lot to do with the bad health of some of the people because it does not have the vitamins in it.
I for one do not believe there is any solution to the butter surplus problem, if it is a problem, by foreign give-away programs or by trying to dump the butter which we have over and above our own needs for the domestic market. I for one would not even favour selling the butter at cut rates behind the iron curtain, as I have heard some people suggest from time to time. I should think that the only thing the Canadian people would not forgive with regard to a price

support program would be this, that in our price support program we accumulated surpluses from which no human being got any benefit. I should think that, if we are trying to get a good sound farm support system, we must be sure that we have no stagnating surpluses, and we must be sure that the butter which enjoys the price support gets to the ultimate consumer. With all respect, I should like to make this suggestion for the consideration of the minister and the consideration of the government. If it should turn out that we have an accumulating surplus, I should like to see careful consideration given to the issuing of coupons to people in a certain amount of need, especially to people on old age assistance in Canada and on war veterans allowance in Canada. These coupons could be issued on a monthly basis.
Last year I had the duty and privilege of looking over the family budgets of a good many hundreds and perhaps even thousands of people living on old age assistance or old age pensions, and I was appalled to learn, after they had their budgets figured to the last cent, how few of these people were able to afford butter. They did not have enough fats; they did not even have enough margarine.
I would suggest to the minister and to the government, with all respect, that if they are considering disposing of the surplus, they do not try to dispose of it behind the iron curtain, that they do not try to dispose of the surplus in Asia, that they do not try to dispose of the surplus in Europe but that they do dispose of the surplus, if and when it occurs, to our own people and on the basis of those who need it most. We could try it out in a most moderate way by experimenting with the group on old age assistance; I refer to the people living on old age pensions with a means test from 65 years of age to 69. If that experiment proves to be sound,-and by that I mean if it is proved that it does not demoralize the regular market for butter; and indeed that is the real test, for whatever we do, it should not take away the profitable sale of butter through the regular channels- and if on a moderate and experimental basis it is proved that it can be done through old age assistance groups, I cannot see any reason why there should not be tried as an experiment, maybe once a year, the issuing of a cheap pound of butter or even a free pound of butter to everybody drawing family allowance, one for every child.
