advocated the amelioration of the flood conditions on the Assiniboine river. I can recall that no longer ago than last summer I had the honour of attending, with the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa and the hon. member for St. Boniface, a meeting with a number of farmers from the Assiniboine river area. At that time the hon. member indicated to that group that he did not consider the flood conditions along the Assiniboine river to be sufficiently grave to justify federal intervention. Consequently I am gratified that the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa has changed his opinion in this regard.
As a matter of fact, this situation along the Assiniboine river has been a real problem to farmers in this locality because, as the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa has pointed out, this river has been in an almost perennial flood condition. It is a fact that in the year 1950 the city of Winnipeg had a narrow escape from total catastrophe owing to the fact that the Assiniboine river did not coincide completely with the Red river in the matter of flood conditions. Had the two coincided, the-city of Winnipeg would have been inundated', completely and would have been under approximately three feet to four feet of water. I suggest that this would be a situation that would be completely catastrophic.
In his remarks subsequent to those of the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa, the minister indicated that this is a situation that deserves a great deal of special consideration on the ground that amelioration would be extremely costly. I would suggest that the cost would be not considerable in comparison with the cost to the country, and particularly the cost to the Winnipeg area, of a catastrophe such as that which I have outlined.

I agree with the minister in this respect. I would suggest that he devote every effort to obtaining that extra appropriation that is required, because it is definitely required and it is certainly justified by the facts of the situation. Here we have a situation of which we had a foretaste in 1950. Those of us who experienced that foretaste have a healthy appreciation of what the situation might have been had the Assiniboine

Supply-Agriculture
coincided with the Red river in flood. We know beyond any shadow of doubt what that situation would have been.
I would suggest to the minister that if he can do anything to protect us and to put into force measures that will give protection against the possibility of such a situation developing in the future, it would be a laudable effort on his part. I hope that he will do so. I believe that the possible economic results of such a catastrophe would be far beyond any possible economic outlay to which the government might be subjected.
The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa gave what I thought was an excellent outline of the facts of the case. I thought he indicated logically the facts of the Assiniboine river and put them forward in a sensible sort of way. One point that he perhaps did not bring forward sufficiently clearly was that this is not an unusual situation but that it is virtually perennial. I can recall that in years gone by, in the vicinity of Poplar Point, almost perennial flood conditions have existed along the Assiniboine river. As was indicated by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa, the farm lands that are threatened by these floods are among the best farm lands in western Canada. Certainly the economic loss that has accrued to these farmers over the years must have been severe. Perhaps that economic loss in the aggregate would amount to far more than the economic investment that might be required to prevent such a situation occurring.
I would therefore urge the minister to do everything in his power to see that the resources of the government are brought to bear to ensure that this Assiniboine river is harnessed as far as flood conditions are concerned. Perhaps, in the harnessing of it, it might be found that the periodic drought that occurs along the western plains in the basin of the Assiniboine river might be contemporaneously ameliorated.

Mr. Chairman, I make no apologies for taking the time of the house to say a few words on behalf of the farmers of my constituency. I want to say at this point that the few lonely trumpets that are blown on behalf of the fruit growers of British Columbia do not pretend in any sense of the word to compete with the very effective 35-piece brass band from the prairies. I happen to represent a lot of small general farmers, fruit farmers, dairy producers and poultry farmers, the type of farmer whose battle with nature has been a somewhat different kind than that of the farmers of the prairie provinces. While prairie farmers have certain climatic hazards and possibly climatic
[Mr. Trainor.l
disadvantages on occasions, the farmers I represent have to work 12 months a year and slave from morning until night on the whole in order to make a living on farms that have been wrested from the forests surrounding them. Therefore I am sure the minister will pay very careful attention to my representations.
As long as you do not think we do not work on the prairies.

I am suggesting there is a difference in the type of work. I had to place the thing somewhat in focus in order to get the minister to appreciate the peculiar difficulties of the farmers I represent. When the minister spoke I was very interested that he repeatedly dealt with the representations made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I was most interested in that because it indicates the growing impact of farm organizations on the government and on public opinion in general. Because of that I cannot fail to mention the fact that the British Columbia federation of agriculture was first organized in 1933 by Mr. Charlie Hayden, Mr. Dodsley Barrow, a former minister of agriculture of the province to whom British Columbia owes a great deal, Mr. Clarence Oldfield and others in the interior of British Columbia. They have done some excellent work throughout the years.
The British Columbia federation is supported by the British Columbia fruit growers association, the Fraser Valley milk producers, the fruit and vegetable producers and the Vancouver island farmers in general. I think they led Canada in advocating the necessity for marketing legislation for the improvement of co-operative marketing, in respect of such things as getting the carbon content of fence wire improved so that the tensile strength of fencing is sufficient, and in arranging for marketing conferences on a provincial basis something along the lines of the federal conferences. They have been interested in getting the federal government to use live vaccine in connection with Newcastle disease. They have been very interested in conservation, taxation and agricultural policies, and all those things that are in the best interests of the farmers in general.
They have also shown a very forward looking approach by the fact that they were the first organization in British Columbia to make representations to the provincial government, which they did in 1950, urging that the water resources of the Columbia river be carefully preserved to the advantage of Canadian interests and that any deals made with the United States should be on the basis

of payment in full in the form of power. I mention these few things because I was active in the early days in the formation of the British Columbia federation of agriculture, and know of its good work.
That organization was the parent organization of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture because in 1935 the late Major Hutton, who came from the interior of British Columbia, went to the Royal Winter Fair at Toronto and at that fair the Canadian Federation of Agriculture was organized. I am very pleased to know that the organization is so well thought of at this time.
I want to pay tribute to the good work that has been done by the members of the federation in British Columbia throughout the years and to the good work being done by the present officers of the federation because, while they work without the publicity of other organizations, the work that is done by the farmers' organization has a tremendous effect on agricultural legislation both provincially and federally. It is true to say that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture was conceived in the interior of British Columbia. Second, it is true to say that the first natural products marketing act established anywhere in Canada was the result of the organization and the activities of the British Columbia fruit growers association. I mention these things to indicate the progressive and constructive approach that the agricultural organizations in the interior of British Columbia and in British Columbia generally have had throughout the years.
The marketing situation in British Columbia has changed considerably in recent years. Prior to the second world war about half the apples grown in British Columbia were marketed in Great Britain. During the second world war thousands of pounds of vegetable seeds such as onions, carrots, beets, lettuce and so on were grown in the southeastern portion of British Columbia particularly and shipped to Great Britain and some other countries. Owing to the shortage of dollars in Great Britain these markets have largely been lost, although we are glad to know there is a slight resumption in the sale of fruit to the British market.
But while these overseas markets have been lost to a considerable extent we are fortunate, owing to the 40 per cent increase in population in British Columbia and the great industrial expansion, that the domestic market in British Columbia has increased considerably and has to some extent offset the loss of the export market in some phases of agriculture. I think it is fair to say that the farmers I represent are doing all they
Sup p ly-A griculture
can to produce high quality produce at a reasonable cost. An increasing number of them are making effective use of labour saving equipment, fertilizers, irrigation and agricultural chemicals. They are also doing what they can as the result of building up efficient co-operative organizations which have a history of good management throughout the years. The farmers I represent and those in British Columbia generally are first of all producing as efficiently as any farmers in Canada, and possibly lead the rest of Canada in the building up of well-managed co-operative organizations to market their produce, particularly through British Columbia Tree Fruits Limited, the interior and coast vegetable marketing boards, the Kootenay cooperative poultry producers, similar organizations representing poultrymen at the coast, and the beef cattle producers.
I say that to indicate that the farmers have not sat back idle but have tried to help themselves as far as possible. They have done the best they can. They have used all facilities available, their energy, capacity, experience and intelligence, to organize some of the best co-operative marketing organizations in Canada at this time. However, regardless of that they are faced at the present time with a problem of increasing costs and falling prices, the same as other farmers in Canada. That means they are facing a very difficult period particularly in certain sections of agriculture.
I am not going to deal at length with that matter, but they need a measure of government action, both on the provincial and federal levels, to assure them the security they are entitled to as a result of the efforts they have made on their own behalf. I think we need adequate provincial and federal marketing legislation which will enable them to develop broad marketing of their own products on a national scale. I think they need a program of price supports which, on general principle, will be available to all farm products if necessary.
I am not going to say any more about the question of floor prices or price supports because other speakers have dealt very fully with that question and have gone into it in detail. I would simply be taking the time of the house by repeating what these speakers have had to say. But I do believe there is a great necessity for an over-all policy of floor prices and price supports to give the farmer the basic security to which he is entitled as a result of helping himself to the fullest extent possible.
Then, we need a national agency with full authority to administer an over-all program of price support under specific terms of reference established by legislation. In addition to that, particularly in British Columbia,

Supply-Agriculture
the fruit industry is of the opinion that provision must be made for establishing whatever import controls may become necessary in connection with administration of price support. These should be of a regional or seasonal nature wherever appropriate. Now, that is all I am going to say with respect to marketing in general.
I want to deal with another question for a few minutes because it is of particular interest to a number of producers that I have the honour to represent. In spite of the growing advances in agriculture in British Columbia there is an urgent need for additional research and extension work designed to promote the production of heavy yields of high quality produce at low cost without impoverishing our soils. It is very necessary in our district because we have very different conditions from those existing on the prairies. We have such changed circumstances, even with climate, within a few miles and our soils vary a great deal even from mile to mile. Generally speaking, many of our soils on which fruit is grown are what is known as benchlands, and are the lighter type of soils which can very quickly be impoverished by poor agricultural practices.
I want to take a minute to draw the minister's attention to a resolution or two passed by the British Columbia fruit growers association in convention on January 18, 19 and 20 of this year at Kelowna. I want to use these two illustrations as an indication of the interest of the farmers of interior British Columbia in an extension of certain research work. One resolution was adopted unanimously at the convention with respect to research in dwarf and semi-dwarf apple tree stocks. The resolution reads as follows, and I am going to place it on the record because it is an important resolution from our point of view:
Whereas many apple plantings in the Okanagan and Kootenays are 30 years of age and older, and
Whereas in the near future considerable replanting will have to be undertaken to replace those trees which are no longer economical producers as well as those producing unmarketable varieties, and
Whereas it is becoming increasingly evident that the pruning, thinning, picking and spraying of standard type trees are both time and material consuming to such an extent that the profit from fruit growing is diminishing even in years of good crops and prices, and
Whereas growers are becoming increasingly interested in dwarf and semi-dwarf stocks such as those from East Mailing,
Therefore be it resolved that this B.C.F.G.A. convention petition the experimental station to place greater emphasis on the propagation and planting of dwarfing stocks in order to find out whether any of our present marketable varieties are incompatible with certain root stocks, and to find the stocks best suited to widely different soil conditions of this area.

The area concerned is the Okanagan and the Kootenays. There is no reflection on the staff of the experimental station at Summer-land which has done excellent work throughout	the years.	The resolution merely
indicates that the staff must have suflflcient funds to carry on that type of research. 1 want particularly to draw the minister's attention to the fact that it is necessary in view of the large replacement of older trees which will be taking place in the Okanagan and Kootenay valleys from now on at an increasing rate.
I now	deal with another resolution
adopted in connection with research because it is of particular interest to the Kootenay district. This is the resolution in connection with little cherry disease. I know the minister's officials have been carrying on research for some years, but it is a serious problem and has caused great loss to some growers. There is a feeling that more extensive research should be carried on in this connection. The resolution adopted by the convention in this regard was:
Whereas development and research work on Kootenay little cherry disease has been carried on for the past eight or more years and while considerable knowledge of this disease has been obtained no solution seems to have been reached in regard to control or eradication nor have varieties been found that are resistant, and
Whereas little cherry disease is becoming an increasingly serious problem each year in the Kootenays and has now appeared in the Wenatchee area south of the international border,
Therefore, be it resolved that this 1955 B.C.F.G.A. convention ask the federal and provincial departments of agriculture to greatly increase the work being done on the little cherry disease and that the ministers of agriculture of both the federal and provincial governments be asked to see that adequate funds are made available for this work.
I am particularly interested in this, Mr. Chairman, because in the Kootenays we have the climate and soil, as well as conditions in general, to produce the finest cherries that can be produced anywhere in Canada. I think that is recognized, particularly so far as Bings, Lamberts and some of the other later varieties are concerned. A number of our cherry growers have suffered severely from little cherry disease, and it is a great impediment to them and the district. Until the disease is conquered the development of the cherry industry in the Kootenays particularly will be retarded because people are somewhat sceptical of putting in new plantings. It is a very important part of our agricultural development in the Kootenay area, so I support in full the representations of the B.C.F.G.A. and ask for further funds for extended research work in this very necessary field.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have another resolution or two passed at the convention, and I

want to deal with one about fruit reaching the market in the best condition, which is a very important thing. This resolution was adopted in that respect:
Whereas it is of the utmost importance that fruit reach the market in the best possible condition, and
Whereas the least bruising will be effected in those railway cars carried nearest the engine,
Therefore be it resolved by this 1955 B.C.F.G.A. convention that all cars of fruit carried by railways be spotted next to the engine.
I mention that to indicate how much consideration they have to give to the handling of fruit by rail transportation. I give credit to the transportation companies and to the officials of the department, both federal and provincial, for the great progress that has been made in recent years in the provision of fast, efficient freight service for the delivery of fruit from the Okanagan and the Kootenay valleys to prairie and other points. I mention this resolution to indicate that there is still room for improvement in this connection.
I want to bring to the minister's attention the question of the shipment of cherries, peaches, apricots and certain soft fruits from the Arrow lakes north to Revelstoke on the main line where that freight is often loaded into fast freight trains which proceed to prairie points. The fruit comes up the Arrow lakes by steamer. It is fairly cool and it is taken care of there. A steamer moving on a large lake provides certain air ventilation and coolness that prevents any deterioration of the fruit. In recent years when it reaches Arrowhead it has been unloaded from this steamer on hot days-and cherries are very susceptible to the heat-and loaded onto the dock at Arrowhead. From there it is loaded into baggage or freight cars and put into the yards at Arrowhead and left there for some time, often in the very strong sun. These cars are then hooked onto a mixed train whose average speed is about 15 miles an hour. Consequently, these fruits are sometimes subjected to very high temperatures for several hours, before reaching Revelstoke. As a result, when they reach the market, sometimes in the case of cherries, they show some development of plum rot or some development of mildew and defects of that sort.
I do urge the minister's officials responsible to do what they can to see that these smaller collecting points get as good service as possible from the railways. Possibly if there were more people living in that area, and the volume of fruit were greater, they would receive more consideration. The points of which I am thinking would not ship more
Supply-Agriculture
than 25 or 35 carloads in a season, but those 25 or 35 carloads are very important to the people concerned.
In the fruit industry of British Columbia in recent years there has been devised a very efficient system of advising growers when to spray-that is, when the trees are in a proper condition, the dormant, the pink blossom, and at other stages. Then there is also an efficient method of advising fruit growers when to pick certain varieties and have them transported to certain points to meet marketing requirements.
This is being done by radio. At the last convention of the British Columbia fruit growers association the matter was discussed, and the following resolution was adopted:
Therefore, be it resolved by this 1955 B.C.F.G.A. convention that the executive of the B.C.F.G.A. make every effort to have this broadcast included in the program of the C.B.C. booster stations at Oliver and Osoyoos.
I would add the booster stations at Creston and Castlegar, and one or two other points. It is also a very necessary and a very worthwhile service to the fruit growers living away from the main lines of transportation. It is useful to them to receive instructions when to spray and pick.
In connection with the question of booster stations I would point out to the minister that the farmers in west Kootenay district are anxious to listen to Canadian radio programs in general. I do hope he will urge the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to erect another two or three booster stations for general service of the farmers in the area I represent.
I see I have only a moment or two left before the hour mentioned for adjournment. I wish to support the remarks of previous speakers with respect to the good effect the price support on butter has had in this country, so far as the dairymen are concerned. I hope the government will continue this policy.
On behalf of the farmers I represent, may I voice my protest against reductions in freight assistance. I have mentioned this on two other occasions, but I feel I should not let this opportunity pass without mentioning it again. It has created considerable hardship to the dairymen and poultrymen particularly in my district.
I see we have almost reached the suggested hour of adjournment, and I shall conclude my remarks at this point in the hope, as usual, that the minister will give serious consideration to the representations I have made.
